1:
"After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was appeased" — the chapter opens on a lull, and the witnesses set the scene on two fronts, the calendar and the providence. The reformed John Gill takes the appeasing of the wrath to have followed quickly, going off with the king's wine within a few days; yet he allows the wider frame the historians favour, that the interval reaches to the return of Xerxes from his expedition into Greece, after which the king gave himself to his amours and, in the seventh year of his reign, married Esther. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the same span with dates: the great feast at Susa fell in 483 B.C., and in the spring of 481 B.C. Xerxes set out for Greece, so the proposal now started belongs somewhere between; the marriage itself, as v.16 will show, did not come about till after the return, the king's long absence explaining the otherwise curious delay.

Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the seed of the whole plot: when the wrath was appeased and the king remembered his harsh treatment of Vashti, his courtiers proposed to fetch fair young virgins from every province to the house of the women in Susa, that he might choose a new queen — a proposal that pleased him and was acted upon.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the bare notice into a meditation on providence. How God put down one that was high and mighty from her seat we read in the chapter before; now we are told how he exalted one of low degree, as the virgin Mary sings in Luke 1:52 and Hannah before her in 1 Sam. 2:4-8. Vashti being humbled for her height, Esther is advanced for her humility. Henry marvels too at the extravagant course taken to please the king: Josephus says that when his anger cooled he grieved over Vashti, but the judgment was irrevocable by the constitution of the realm, so his servants contrived to make him forget her with a variety of concubines and then fix him upon the most agreeable of them for a wife. The marriages of princes, Henry observes, are commonly made by policy and interest, for enlarging dominions and strengthening alliances; but this must be made by the mere agreeableness of the person to the king's fancy, whether she were rich or poor, noble or ignoble — as if his power and wealth were given him for no other end than to wind the delights of sense up to their height, which at the best are but dross and dregs beside divine and spiritual pleasures. The witnesses do not divide; between Gill's and Ellicott's chronology and Henry's theology they frame a chapter in which the vanity of a heathen court becomes, all unknowing, the cradle of Israel's deliverance.
2:
The proposal itself comes from the king's attendants, and the witnesses ask both why they spoke and what they urged. The reformed John Gill suspects their motive: fearing that if Vashti were restored she would take vengeance on them, and wishing to lift the king out of his melancholy, the servants who ministered to him ventured the advice that follows. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke describes the thing advised as the ordinary way an Eastern harem was furnished — the finest women of the land, whether of high or low birth, sought out and brought in; all became the king's concubines, but one was to be raised as chief wife, the sultana upon the throne, and her issue specially entitled to inherit. It is the way of an absolute court, on his account: the whole empire is ransacked for its fairest, and out of that multitude a single favourite lifted to reign, the rest kept as inferior wives.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the proposal in full: fair young virgins to be sought, officers appointed in all the provinces to gather them to Shushan the palace, to the house of the women under the custody of the king's chamberlain, their things for purification given them, and the maiden who pleased the king to be made queen instead of Vashti — a plan that pleased the king, and he did so.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the pains taken to humour a sensual prince, and will not let the reader mistake such a scheme for happiness. What pains were taken to please the king! — as if all his greatness were bestowed only that the pleasures of sense might be refined to their utmost. Those destitute of divine revelation, he says, and given up as a punishment for their idolatry to vile affections, broke through the law of creation founded upon God's making one man and one woman; there was need of the gospel of Christ to purify men from the lusts of the flesh and reduce them to the original institution, so that those who have learned Christ think it a shame even to speak of such things as were here done openly, as Eph. 5:12 has it. Yet Henry bids us look past the vanity to the wise and merciful providence of God, carrying on his deep but holy designs in the midst of it all. The witnesses converge: Gill reads the courtiers' fear, Clarke the custom of the seraglio, Keil and Delitzsch the terms of the plan, and Henry the sin and the overruling grace woven silently through it.
3:
The plan's machinery occupies this verse — officers, a gathering, a keeper, and a long purifying — and the witnesses attend to each part. The reformed John Gill notes that the officers appointed in every province were those who best knew where the beautiful virgins of their district might be found. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies the house of the women as the harem, then as now a prominent feature of an Eastern king's establishment, and distinguishes its keepers: Hege, the Hegai of v.8, had charge of the virgins, while another, the Shaashgaz of v.14, kept the concubines. The whole verse, Ellicott adds, shows in how degrading a light Eastern women were viewed as a whole; it was reserved for Christianity to indicate the true position of woman — not man's plaything, but the help meet for him, yielding intelligent obedience rather than slavery.

The wesleyan-arminian voices fill in the officers and the ointments. Adam Clarke reads "the king's chamberlain" as the king's eunuch, for in the East the women were entrusted to eunuchs only; the "things for purification" are their cosmetics, the oil of myrrh and sweet odours named at v.12, six months of the one and six of the other, a space long enough to prove the young woman chaste and free the king from fathering a spurious child — though the Targum, he notes, makes it oil of unripe olives, which caused the hair to fall and the skin to grow delicate. John Wesley adds that the chamberlain was keeper of all the women, both virgins and concubines, but took the virgins into his own more careful charge and left the concubines to Shaashgaz his deputy; the purifying was to cleanse them of every impurity, to perfume, adorn, and prepare them for the king — for the legal purification of the Jews he never regarded.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the scheme into a single scornful inventory: all the provinces searched for fair young virgins and officers set to choose them; a house prepared on purpose and a person charged to keep them; twelve whole months allowed for their purifying, that even the masterpieces of nature might yet have all the help of art to recommend them to a vain and carnal mind. The witnesses do not divide over the facts; together they lay bare a court in which a whole empire is ransacked to gratify one man, and in which — though none there knows it — a captive orphan is being drawn toward a throne.
4:
"And let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti" — the counsellors' proposal reaches its point, and the witnesses fix on the crown it offers. The reformed John Gill reads the promise plainly: the royal estate taken from Vashti is to be given to whichever maiden pleases the king, the very crown set upon her head. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add the two clauses that close the advice — "the thing pleased the king, and he did so" — so that the whole scheme, from the search to the coronation, is set in motion by a word that fell in with the king's own humour.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks what kind of queen this would be: of all the women brought to the harem, one was to be lifted above the rest as chief wife and sultana, her issue specially entitled to inherit the throne — a real elevation, not a passing favour. Gill, marking the same crown, says the royal estate taken from Vashti was simply to pass to another, the diadem set on a new head, so that the disgrace of the one queen becomes the opportunity of the next.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns from the mechanism to the providence and to a defence of Esther's honour. Here, he says, was the overruling providence of God bringing Esther to be queen: had she been recommended to Ahasuerus for a wife he would have rejected the motion with disdain, but coming in her turn, after many others, and excelling them all, way was made for her even by her rivals into the king's affections. Providence, he adds, sometimes raiseth up the poor out of the dust to set them among princes, as Hannah sang in 1 Sam. 2:8. And Henry meets, on the authority of Bishop Patrick, those who suggest that Esther sinned to reach this dignity: they do not consider the custom of those times and countries, for every one the king took to his bed was married to him and was his wife of a lower rank, as Hagar was Abraham's; so that, had she never been made queen, the sons of Jacob need not have said he dealt with their sister as with a harlot. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch trace the plan and its acceptance, Clarke the rank it promised, and Henry the hidden hand that would fill Vashti's empty place — not with one of the empire's noble daughters, but with a Jewess of the captivity whom God had marked for the deliverance of her people.
5:
Now the narrative pauses to introduce the man on whom so much will turn, and the witnesses gather around his name, his lineage, and his character. The reformed John Gill explains why a Benjamite is called "a certain Jew": not that he was of the tribe of Judah, but that he belonged to the kingdom of Judah, and, as Jarchi notes, all who were carried captive with the kings of Judah were called Jews among the nations, whatever their tribe. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply set him in Shushan the palace — Mordecai the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite — before the story of his foster-daughter is told.

Over the genealogy the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the Targum's romance: that this Shimei was the very man who cursed David, whom David forbade Joab to slay because he foresaw in the spirit of prophecy that Shimei would be the ancestor of Esther and Mordecai. Charles Ellicott weighs the same names more soberly: probably they are the actual father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of Mordecai, though some take Shimei for David's assailant and Kish for the father of Saul.

But Ellicott parts sharply from his fellows over the man himself, and here a real disagreement opens. Following Canon Rawlinson, he is disposed to identify Mordecai with Matacas, the most powerful of Xerxes' eunuchs, and thinks it may be assumed that Mordecai was a eunuch, from the freedom with which he was allowed access to the royal harem in v.11 and v.22. More than this, he reads the character darkly: an ambitious, worldly man who, though numbers of his tribe had returned to the land of their fathers, preferred to remain on alien soil; not for him the heroic lament of the exiles by Babel's streams who would not sing the Lord's song in a strange land, but rather the calculation that his adopted daughter's beauty might catch the eye of a sensual king and make her guardian the king's chief minister. Neither Gill nor Clarke nor the later course of the book bears out so harsh a portrait, and the other witnesses leave Mordecai simply a Jew of the captivity, keeper of his orphaned cousin. The name itself, Ellicott observes, appears among those who returned with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2:2 and Neh. 7:7 — a thread that ties this courtier, however he is judged, to the whole restored remnant.
6:
The parenthesis about the captivity raises a small chronological puzzle, and the witnesses solve it the same way. The verse says the man "had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away," and the reformed John Gill argues that this must be joined not to Mordecai but to his great-grandfather Kish; for were Mordecai himself the captive, he would now be a very old man, and Esther, his cousin, far too old to be reckoned among the young virgins or so admired for her beauty — the former Targum, he notes, makes her seventy-five, which is not to be believed. Mordecai and Esther being the children of two brothers, Gill reasons, they must be near enough in age that, if the aged Mordecai had himself endured the deportation, his cousin could hardly be the young and lovely maiden the story requires; the captivity, therefore, belongs to the ancestor and not to the man himself.

The grammatical-historical witnesses reach the same conclusion by grammar and arithmetic. Charles Ellicott allows that, as far as the bare syntax goes, the antecedent might be Mordecai, but it is obviously Kish; Jeconiah is Jehoiachin, whose deportation, recorded in 2 Kings 24:12-16, fell in 598 B.C., a hundred and seventeen years before this time, so that the four generations from Kish to Mordecai are readily accounted for. Keil and Delitzsch carry the same captivity-notice forward into the account of Esther that follows, treating it as the pedigree that stamps both cousins as children of the exile — the deportation under which Nebuchadnezzar had led Jeconiah and the flower of Jerusalem to Babylon.

The point is not a dry one, for the witnesses see in it the quiet dignity of the whole story. The queen God is about to raise is no native Persian but the descendant of a family torn from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar; the throne of the empire that will presently threaten the Jews is to be shared by one of the very captives that empire's forerunner had dragged into bondage. Gill guards the chronology so that Esther may be young and fair as the narrative requires; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch anchor the family in a datable deportation; and together they make certain that the reader never forgets, amid the splendour of Susa, that this is a daughter of the captivity being led, by an unseen hand, toward a crown.
7:
The verse names its heroine twice over and tells her whole condition in a breath — an orphan, a beauty, a cousin taken as a daughter — and the witnesses linger over each. On the double name they largely agree. The reformed John Gill gives Hadassah as "myrtle," the tree to which good Israelites are sometimes likened, and derives Esther either from a root meaning "to hide," since Mordecai hid her kindred, or from the Persian word for a star, even the star of Venus. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make Esther the Old-Persian stara with a prosthetic aleph, answering to the Greek aster and the modern Persian sitareh; the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls Hadassah her first, Babylonish name and Esther undoubtedly Persian; Charles Ellicott sees in the two names an early case of the common Jewish practice of bearing both a Hebrew and a Gentile name, as Saul was Paul and John was Mark; and John Wesley notes simply that Hadassah was her name before her marriage and Esther the name the king gave her after. Gill alone ventures further, toying with the guess that she was the Amestris whom Xerxes married, only to record the objections that stand against it.

On her kindred the witnesses are one. She was the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, and therefore his cousin — not his niece, Clarke insists, whatever the Vulgate and Josephus say; and having neither father nor mother, she was taken by Mordecai, when her parents died, for his own daughter and brought up as his foster-child.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the pathos and the lessons out of these few facts. She was one of the children of the captivity, a sharer in her people's bondage; she was an orphan, but "when her father and mother forsook her, then the Lord took her up," as Ps. 27:10 has it; she was a beauty, though her wisdom and virtue were her greater beauty — yet it is an advantage to a diamond to be well set. Mordecai her guardian took her for his own; the Septuagint, Henry notes, says he meant to make her his wife, and if so he is to be praised that he did not oppose her better preferment. Let God be acknowledged, Henry urges, in raising up friends for the fatherless, and let those who take charge of orphans look, like Mordecai, to see the good fruit of their care. Dr. Lightfoot even thought this Mordecai the same who went up with the first returning exiles in Ezra 2:2 and afterwards came back to the Persian court. The witnesses leave Esther as Scripture sets her: a fatherless captive of surpassing grace, whom Providence has already, through a kinsman's kindness, been quietly preparing.
8:
When the decree went out, the gathering it commanded swept Esther up with the rest, and the witnesses trace how she came to the king's house. The reformed John Gill marks only that the king's commandment and decree were heard throughout the several provinces of his kingdom — the summons proclaimed to every corner of the realm, so that the levy of maidens reached even the household where a captive's daughter was quietly kept. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence on: when the commandment was published and many maidens were gathered together to Shushan, Esther also was received into the royal harem under the keeping of Hegai, brought in among the crowd of candidates that the officers of v.3 had assembled.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, surveying the chapter, sets this moment in its sequence: Esther is chosen among the young women and placed under the care of Hegai the king's chamberlain, there to begin the long year of purifying that the law of the women required. The gathering, on his reading, is no gentle invitation but a conscription of the empire's fairest, and Esther is one taken up in it, whether her guardian would or no. Once received, Clarke notes, she was set under Hegai to begin the year of purifying, the same appointed course through which every candidate must pass before she could be brought in.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the finger of God in the very ordinariness of her being "brought." Who would have thought, he exclaims, that a Jewess, a captive, and an orphan was born to be a queen, an empress? Yet so it proved; for Providence sometimes raises the poor out of the dust to set them among princes, as Hannah sang in 1 Sam. 2:8. Had Esther been pressed upon the king as a suitor for his hand, Henry observes, he would have disdained the motion; but coming in her turn, one among many, way was quietly made for her by the very competition that seemed to bury her. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the proclamation, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke the assembling and Esther's reception under Hegai, and Henry the providence that used a heathen king's roving desire as the road by which a captive child should climb, unsuspected, toward the throne of her people's oppressor. What looks like the caprice of an idle court is, to these readers, the opening move of a deliverance already determined in heaven.
9:
No sooner is Esther brought in than she wins the heart of her keeper, and the witnesses ask who was pleased and why. The reformed John Gill is careful that it was not yet the king — into whose presence she had not come — but the chamberlain who was taken with her; her beauty and her behaviour together recommended her, so that he concluded within himself that she of all would prove acceptable to the king. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the favour in the Hebrew idiom of "bearing away kindness," and list what it won her: he hastened to give her the things for her purifying and her portion, seven chosen maidens out of the king's house, and the best place in the house of the women for her and her maids. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same partiality: Hegai conceived a preference for her above the rest, most likely for the propriety of her deportment and her unassuming manners, and the seven maidens were to attend her to the bath, to anoint and adorn her, and be her servants. Charles Ellicott notes that the phrase for her winning "kindness" is the very same rendered "obtained favour in his sight" of the king himself at v.17 — the servant's regard foreshadowing the master's.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley will not leave the favour to nature alone. She pleased the keeper because she was very beautiful, so that he supposed she would be acceptable to the king; but it was also, Wesley insists, by the divine power which moves the hearts of men whichever way God pleases. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry says the same in his own key: the king's chamberlain honoured her, for wisdom and virtue will gain respect, and those who make sure of God's favour shall find favour with men too, so far as it is good for them.

Here too the witnesses divide their emphasis without contradiction. Gill and Clarke credit her manners and modesty, Keil and Delitzsch count the gifts her favour drew, Ellicott hears the coming crown already echoed in the keeper's kindness, and Wesley and Henry trace the whole to the God who was turning a Persian courtier's liking to the service of his hidden purpose. The favour Esther finds is real and deserved, yet the witnesses agree it is also given — a first token that the hand which raised her worked as much through the affections of those about her as through her own excelling grace.
10:
Behind Esther's rising favour lies a silence she has been charged to keep, and the witnesses probe both the fact and its reason. The reformed John Gill observes that she had not shown her people nor her kindred; being unasked, she was under no obligation to declare it, and, born most likely in Shushan, she was taken for a native Persian. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the notice as a supplementary remark explaining the very kindness she met: such friendly usage would hardly have fallen to a Jewish maiden, so it was in obedience to Mordecai's charge that she hid her Jewish extraction.

Why Mordecai laid that charge the witnesses variously judge, though they do not quarrel. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke thinks a known Jewish birth might have prejudiced the king, for it was no credit at the Persian court to be a Jew, and envy of her origin might have barred her access altogether. Charles Ellicott reads it as Mordecai's hope that she might pass for a native Persian, her descent proving no hindrance to her advancement — and notes that the king does not learn his wife's nation until far later, at Esther 7:4. John Wesley adds a deeper reason still: lest the knowledge should make her contemptible or bring some inconvenience upon the whole nation; yet there was also a hand of God in the concealment, for the better accomplishing of what he designed, though Mordecai himself was ignorant of it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry guards the ethics of the silence with care. Mordecai did not bid her deny her country, nor tell a lie to conceal her parentage — had he told her so, she must not have obeyed; he only charged her not to proclaim it. All truths, Henry allows, are not to be spoken at all times, though an untruth is not to be spoken at any time; and Esther, taken by all for a Persian, was not bound to undeceive them. The witnesses land together on a concealment that is prudent without being false: Gill and Ellicott make it the natural cover of one born in Shushan, Clarke the shield against court prejudice, Wesley the veil of providence over a chosen instrument, and Henry the careful distinction between hiding a truth and speaking a lie. What none of them doubts is that the secret was kept by God's design as much as Mordecai's, held in reserve for the hour when its disclosure would save a people.
11:
Even after Esther passes within the palace walls, her guardian keeps his daily watch, and the witnesses read his pacing as the mark of a faithful love. The reformed John Gill supposes that Mordecai, being himself of the court and in some high post — as Aben Ezra thought — could walk before the court of the women's house without being challenged or called to account. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the same constancy: every day Mordecai walked before the enclosure of the women's house to learn Esther's welfare and what was being done with her, so that he kept up an unbroken communication with her even after she entered the harem. Charles Ellicott, from the same freedom of access, infers that Mordecai was apparently one of the royal doorkeepers, a station confirmed by his sitting in the king's gate at v.21 and named again at Esther 5:13. It is by this daily attendance, Keil and Delitzsch add, that Mordecai was able to keep in constant touch with his cousin, learning through the servants of the house how it went with her.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the daily walk into a picture of guardianship. Mordecai was tender of Esther as if she had been his own child, walking before her door every day to know how she did and what interest she had; and let those, Henry urges, whose relations are cast upon them by divine Providence be as kindly affectioned and as solicitous for them. The care is unglamorous — a man pacing a courtyard for news of a girl who can send him none openly — and precisely in that unglamorous constancy the witnesses find its worth.

They do not divide. Gill and Ellicott explain how his office let him keep so near; Keil and Delitzsch mark the steady channel of intelligence it preserved; Henry draws the lesson of a foster-father's love. And all of them see in the arrangement more than sentiment: because Mordecai walks there daily, he will be in place to overhear a plot in v.21 and, through Esther, to save the king; because the channel between guardian and queen stays open, the whole later deliverance of the Jews will have its line of communication ready-made. The verse looks like a note of private affection, but the witnesses see providence laying its quiet groundwork, keeping Mordecai at the one post from which he can serve both the throne and his people when the moment comes.
12:
The narrative slows to describe the long ritual that preceded every maiden's single night, and the witnesses attend to its length and its purpose. The reformed John Gill explains that each maid's turn came only after twelve months "according to the manner of women," the candidates going in by the order of their time in the house, as Herodotus reports of the wives of the Persian kings. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the calendar exactly: twelve months of preparation, six with oil of myrrh and six with balsam and the ointments of purifying, after which, when her turn came, whatever she desired was given her to take from the women's house to the king's. Charles Ellicott adds a philological touch, that the word our version renders "manner" is rather "law" or "ordinance," the same term used of the fixed usage of the court in Esther 1:8 — so that this whole year was no casual custom but a prescribed rule binding on every maiden alike.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers the boldest explanation of so long a regimen, and stands somewhat alone in it. The fairest virgins were drawn indiscriminately from every class, many reared in low life on coarse, strong food that breeds a heavy and sometimes unpleasant odour of the skin; a full year of wholesome diet, frequent hot baths, and the body often rubbed with oil would in almost every case sweeten and refine it, giving healthy action to the vessels of the skin and promoting health and comfort throughout. Where the others see only luxury, Clarke sees hygiene and physic.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees chiefly the vanity of it. No less than twelve months, he marvels, was allowed for their purifying, that even the masterpieces of nature might have all the help of art to recommend them to a vain and carnal mind. The witnesses do not so much contradict one another as light the same custom from different sides: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the order and the calendar of the myrrh and the spices, Ellicott sharpens the legal word behind "manner," Clarke ventures a physician's rationale for the year's length, and Henry moralizes the whole as art lavished upon flesh. Beneath their differences lies one quiet fact they all let stand — that Esther too passed through this year, and that when at last her turn came she would ask for none of the finery the custom pressed upon the rest.
13:
When the year was over, each maiden went to the king on terms the verse now sets down, and the witnesses mark the strange licence of it. The reformed John Gill notes only that this was the way every virgin came, her twelve months of purifying accomplished. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch spell out the provision: whatever she asked was given her to take with her from the house of the women to the king's house — she went in the evening and returned in the morning to a second house of the women, under the keeping of Shaashgaz who kept the concubines, and came to the king no more unless he delighted in her and called her by name. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same grant of "whatsoever she desired" as an ordinance that any dress, colour, or jewels she thought would best set off her person should be given her — each maiden free to adorn herself to the utmost for her one appearance, taking with her out of the women's house whatever she thought would most commend her to the king.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the desired things as ornament or attendance, and pauses, as he often does, over the moral standing of the whole business. Every one whom the king took to his bed, he observes, was his wife of a lower rank, as Hagar was Abraham's; so that it would have been no sin nor dishonour to Esther even had she not been made queen — a defence of her that echoes what the other witnesses say of the custom of those times.

The witnesses do not divide over the facts, and the picture they draw is a sombre one. A year's pains, a single night, and then, for all but one, the second house and the long silence of the concubines' quarters, never to see the king's face again unless he should chance to remember a name. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch trace the mechanism, Clarke the freedom to adorn, Wesley the lawfulness of Esther's place within it; and all of them leave the reader to feel, behind the pomp, the waste and the sadness of a court where women were gathered by the hundred to gratify one man and then set aside. It is into this that Esther must go — and out of it, alone, that she will be lifted.
14:
The verse follows the maidens into the aftermath of their night, and the witnesses dwell on the closed world that received them. The reformed John Gill identifies the "second house of the women" as the other apartment, where those the king had made his concubines were kept — Aben Ezra reading it rather "the second time," or "again." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence to its bleak end: in the evening she went to the king, and in the morning returned to this second house, to the hand of Shaashgaz who kept the concubines, and came to him no more except he delighted in her and she were called by name.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the fate such women met: kept apart in that second house, they went out no more and were never given in marriage to any man, nor saw the king's face again unless specially summoned. He turns even the keeper's name to account, taking Shaashgaz for a Persian word meaning "beardless," a fitting epithet for a eunuch, or else "weak loins" to the same effect — names, he remarks, that show their own reason in describing the man's condition. Gill, weighing the same phrase, allows that Aben Ezra would render it not "the second house" but "the second time," or "again," as though the maiden simply returned once more to the women's quarters — but the drift is the same, that she passed from the king's chamber into a settled and separate keeping.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the arrangement as the token of a whole disordered estate. After the king had once taken them, he notes, they were made recluses ever after, save when he pleased to send for them; reckoned as secondary wives, maintained accordingly, and forbidden to marry. In this Henry sees to what absurd practices those came who were destitute of divine revelation, given up as a punishment for their idolatry to affections that broke the law of one man and one woman written into creation itself. The witnesses do not divide; Gill and Keil and Delitzsch describe the second house and its keeper, Clarke the sealed and marriageless future of its inmates, Henry the moral ruin the custom betrays. Together they make the concubines' quarters a silent foil to Esther's coming exaltation: the many are gathered, used, and shut away nameless, while one alone is drawn out of the crowd to be crowned — a contrast the witnesses let stand without needing to underline it.
15:
When at last Esther's own turn came, she went to the king in a way that set her apart from every maiden before her, and the witnesses fasten on her restraint. The reformed John Gill pauses first on her parentage, naming her the daughter of Abihail — not Aminadab, as the Septuagint has it — and Mordecai's cousin whom he had taken for his daughter. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark what she carried in: she required nothing but what Hegai the keeper of the women appointed, plainly unconcerned to win the king by any special adornment, and so she obtained favour in the sight of all who looked upon her, by her modesty and humility. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same self-forgetfulness: she left the matter wholly to her friend Hegai's judgment, and went in only the dress and the ornaments he deemed most suitable, trusting his care rather than her own art.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes her reticence the very secret of her charm. She was not solicitous, as the rest of the maidens were, to set herself off with artificial beauty, but asked for nothing beyond what was appointed her — and yet she was the most acceptable of them all, for the more natural beauty is, the more agreeable. All that looked upon her admired her, Henry adds, and concluded she was the one who would win the prize; and she did win it. Her humility, in his reading, is not a foil to her beauty but its finest setting; the diamond needs no gilding that is already well cut.

The witnesses do not divide, and they draw from her restraint a lesson the court could not teach. Where every other maiden lavished a year's art on a single night, Esther trusted herself to another's judgment and asked for nothing; and precisely that trust, the witnesses agree, was what drew every eye and, in the end, the king's. What the others heaped on by artifice, she gained by asking for nothing at all. Gill fixes her lineage and her guardian, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke her deference to Hegai, Henry the paradox that the plainest candidate proved the most winning. Behind their common admiration lies the same conviction that has run through the chapter: that the favour Esther finds she does not manufacture but receives, and that the hand appointing her a keeper's guidance is the same hand that has appointed her a crown.
16:
The verse fixes the hour of Esther's summons with unusual precision, and the witnesses read both the date and the difference of her going. The reformed John Gill marks that she did not return next morning to the house of the women, as the concubines did, but was taken to be the king's wife and kept in a fitting apartment, designed already for the dignity to which she was rising. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that she was taken into the royal residence in the tenth month, the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of Ahasuerus' reign. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke glosses Tebeth as answering to part of our December and January; Charles Ellicott sets it more nearly at January or February of 478 B.C., very shortly after Xerxes' return to Susa from the west, and explains the long delay in replacing Vashti simply by the king's protracted absence in Greece. The month, he observes, answers to the Egyptian Tybi, and the season of her taking must have fallen very shortly after Xerxes came home from the west, when at last the vacant throne could be filled.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry does the arithmetic the date invites. This was done in the king's seventh year, and Vashti had been divorced in his third, as Esther 1:3 records; so that Ahasuerus was some four years without a queen — a gap the other witnesses fill with his campaign abroad. Henry's interest, though, is less in the calendar than in the swiftness of the king's decision once Esther appeared: he needed now to make no further trials, nor take time to deliberate, but was soon determined.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill marks that Esther alone, of all the maidens, was retained rather than dismissed to the concubines' house; Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke and Ellicott fix the month and the year and account for the delay by the war in Greece; Henry measures the four empty years and the king's ready choice. Behind the exact dating the readers sense the patience of providence: for four years the throne beside Ahasuerus stood vacant, through a great king's long absence and a whole empire's fruitless search, until in the depth of a winter month, the tenth, the one whom God had prepared was at last brought in — and the vacancy that had waited so long was filled in a single evening.
17:
The climax of Esther's rise falls in this verse, and the witnesses gather at the moment the crown is set on her head. The reformed John Gill reads that the king loved Esther above all the women — the virgins he had taken and made his concubines — though Jarchi, he notes, would include married women among those gathered too. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch state the plain sense: immediately upon their first meeting the king bestowed his affection on Esther above all the women and maidens, so that she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins, and he set the royal crown upon her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks what that crown meant in an Eastern court: it made her the Sultana, the queen, mistress of all the rest of the wives, who were bound thenceforth to pay her the most profound respect — no longer one candidate among many, but the crowned head to whom the whole household of women must bow.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the turn on which the whole providence swings. The king loved Esther above all the women; now, Henry says, he needed to make no further trials nor take time to deliberate, but was soon determined to set the royal crown upon her head and make her queen. The captive orphan of the earlier verses, the Jewess who had asked for no adornment, is lifted in a moment above every rival and every wife in the empire.

The witnesses do not divide; they simply weigh the same wonder from their several stations. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the king's love and the setting of the crown, Clarke the sovereign rank it conferred, Henry the decisiveness with which a deliberating king was fixed at last. And under all their words runs the note the chapter has been sounding from its first verse — that the exalting of Esther is God's doing before it is Ahasuerus'; the love the king feels above all reason, the choice he makes without further trial, and the crown he sets on her head, are, to these readers, the visible face of an invisible appointment, by which a daughter of the captivity is set on the throne of Persia against the very hour her people will need a queen at the king's side.
18:
Esther's coronation is crowned in turn with a feast and a public largess, and here the witnesses openly divide over what the king's "release" to the provinces was. The reformed John Gill takes the great feast to the nobles and servants as Ahasuerus' marriage-banquet, which the Greek makes seven days long and Josephus a whole month. But over the "release" the readings part. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the Hebrew word, rendered by the Greek and Latin as a "rest," and judge it, from the force of the verb, to mean not a remission of taxes but a holiday, a day of release from labour, though they grant the Chaldee took it of taxes. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it rather as a remittance of tribute or impost granted at the coronation, as kings at their crowning release prisoners; he thinks especially of the "queen-gold," the tenth of fines that Persian queens received, from which Esther may have wished certain cities relieved, to make her the more popular.

Charles Ellicott renders the word literally "rest" and holds it a release either from tribute or from military service, probably the former, as consistent with Persian usage. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry offers yet a third sense, that the release was either a remittance of taxes in arrear or an act of grace for criminals — as Pilate at the feast released a prisoner — a thing done to add to the public joy. So the question stands genuinely open among them: was the king's boon a holiday from work, a remission of taxes, a release of prisoners, or a lifting of tribute and military service?

On the rest of the verse the witnesses agree. Keil and Delitzsch note that the king gave gifts with royal munificence, and remark how strange it is that four years should divide Vashti's fall from Esther's rise — a gap the chapter's own dates leave to be explained by the war abroad. Henry adds that Esther, in compliance with the king, likely made at her coronation-feast the public appearance Vashti had refused, gaining the praise of obedience in the very instance where the other had earned the blot of disobedience. The debate over the "release" the witnesses leave unsettled; what they do not doubt is that the whole realm was made to keep holiday for the raising of a queen whose true errand none of them yet knew.
19:
A second gathering of virgins is named almost in passing, and the witnesses puzzle over what it can mean so long after a queen was crowned. The reformed John Gill rejects the notion that this "second time" looks back to some earlier collection in Vashti's day, of which nothing is recorded; he reads it rather as a fresh assembling for the king's pleasure, whose lust was not satisfied though he had both a queen he loved and his house of concubines. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confess the phrase obscure: no reason can be seen for gathering maidens a second time after the king's choice had already fallen on Esther, and yet the words plainly fix the time of the conspiracy that follows. Charles Ellicott presses the difficulty into a comment on the king's character: within less than five years of taking Esther "above all the women," there takes place a second gathering of virgins like the first, so degraded is the "love" the earlier verse spoke of; and he would read the next verse as a parenthesis, joining the conspiracy of v.21 closely to this nineteenth. There is no article in the Hebrew, he adds, so it is simply "virgins," another gathering like the first; and the whole incident falls at some unfixed point between Esther's marriage and the twelfth year of the reign named in Esther 3:7.

Set within the same verse is the first notice of Mordecai's post, and here the witnesses agree. Mordecai sat in the king's gate — by office, the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains, as one of the king's guards or ministers, advanced to the place, he thinks, by Esther's favour. Ellicott, rendering it "Mordecai was sitting," takes the gate for the station of a royal official, the vantage from which the plot will presently be overheard.

The witnesses do not resolve the riddle of the second gathering so much as register it honestly. Gill makes it the overflow of a sensual king's appetite, Keil and Delitzsch own it simply dark, Ellicott turns it into evidence of how little the king's professed love was worth. What all of them see is the deft hinge the verse provides: by fixing "in those days," when maidens were again assembled and Mordecai sat in the gate, the historian sets the stage for the service that will bind the king to Mordecai and, long after, deliver the Jews. The obscure notice and the seated doorkeeper are, in their hands, the quiet apparatus by which providence prepares its next stroke.
20:
The historian pauses to record that Esther, though a queen, still keeps her guardian's two commands — her secret and her obedience — and the witnesses read in her constancy the mark of her character. The reformed John Gill notes that she had not shown her kindred nor her people, neither before nor since she was made queen; the Targum, he adds, will have it that the king himself pressed her to tell, and still she held her peace. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as resuming the thread after the notice of the gathering, and read its heart in the clause that Esther did the commandment of Mordecai still, exactly as when she was brought up under his care — her elevation changing nothing of her deference. Charles Ellicott suggests the verse is set here to meet a natural supposition, that the king might have wished to replace Esther on discovering her nation; her secret, still kept, forestalls the danger.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes her continued obedience the ornament of her greatness. Though advanced to the throne, Esther still did the commandment of Mordecai as when she was a child in his house; and this, Henry says, was clear evidence of a humble and grateful disposition, that she kept the sense of his former kindnesses and his continued wisdom. It is a great ornament to those who are raised, he adds, and much to their praise, to remember their benefactors, to retain the good impressions of their education, to be diffident of themselves and willing still to take advice. Mordecai for his part sat contentedly in the king's gate, aiming no higher, and yet the queen upon the throne remained observant of him.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the kept secret and its prudence, Keil and Delitzsch the unbroken obedience, Henry the humility that obedience displays. And all of them see the two things held together in the verse — the concealed people and the honoured guardian — as the double thread from which the deliverance will be woven: a queen who still keeps her origin hidden until the appointed hour, and who still heeds the one man through whom God will speak to her when that hour comes. Esther's greatness, in their reading, is safest precisely because it has not made her forget either where she came from or whom she must obey.
21:
The chapter's last movement turns from the palace to a plot against the throne, and the witnesses read Mordecai's post and the traitors' malice as the stuff of providence. The reformed John Gill marks simply that Mordecai sat in the king's gate, being, as already observed, an officer at court. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes up the thread from v.19 — "in those days," while Mordecai sat there — and notes the grim aptness of the danger: two of the king's chamberlains, keepers of the threshold, were wroth and sought to lay hands on Ahasuerus, and it is worth remembering, he observes, that Xerxes was in the end actually murdered by a captain of the guard and a chamberlain. He fixes the names too, the Bigthan here being the Bigtha of Esther 1:10 and the Bigthana of Esther 6:2.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke asks why the two conspired, and reports the Targum's guess that they had learned Esther meant to use her influence to remove them and set Mordecai in their place, and so resolved to poison her and slay the king in his bedchamber; Clarke thinks it likely they were creatures of Haman, employed to open his own way to the throne. Whatever the cause, he notes that Mordecai, sitting in the gate, was well placed as an officer of some standing, not a mere porter — for had he been only a doorkeeper, Haman could later have removed him at will.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole incident as a step in a design larger than the plotters knew. No move has yet been made toward Haman's scheme against the Jews, Henry says, but several are here made toward God's design for their deliverance, and this for one: God now gives Mordecai the chance to do the king a good turn, that he may have the fairer opportunity, afterwards, to do the Jews a good turn. Princes, above other men, carry their lives in their hands and are the mark of much ill-will; so two of his own servants, resenting some affront or injury, sought not merely to imprison but to kill him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott set Mordecai in the gate and name the traitors, Clarke searches out their motive, Henry lifts the plot into the counsel of God — where a conspiracy meant to end one reign becomes, unforeseen, the first stone laid toward the rescue of a people.
22:
How the plot came to light, and what Mordecai did with it, occupy the witnesses next, and they trade the several traditions of its discovery. The reformed John Gill owns that the text does not say by what means the thing became known to Mordecai, and gathers the guesses: the Jewish writers make the two conspirators Tarsians who plotted in their own tongue, thinking Mordecai did not understand it, though he, skilled in languages, overheard them; Josephus has it revealed by one Barnabazus, a servant of one of the chamberlains; while the later Targum simply ascribes the discovery to the Holy Ghost, as though heaven itself had whispered the secret into a faithful ear. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke follows Josephus's version, that a Jew named Barnabasus overheard the plot, told it to Mordecai, Mordecai to Esther, and Esther to the king in Mordecai's name.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep to what the verse plainly states: the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it to Esther the queen, and Esther certified the king of it in Mordecai's name — the open channel between guardian and queen, kept up since v.11, now bearing its first great fruit. Charles Ellicott draws out the consequence: by this service an increased influence was doubtless gained over the capricious mind of the king, an influence which before long would serve Esther in good stead, when she must venture uninvited into that same king's presence.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance. However the plot was overheard — by Mordecai's own ear, by a servant's whisper, or, as the Targum piously says, by the Spirit of God — all agree it passed at once from Mordecai to Esther and from Esther to the king, and always in Mordecai's name, so that the credit was faithfully preserved, and Mordecai's name attached to the deed in the hearing of the throne. Gill and Clarke rehearse the manner of the discovery, Keil and Delitzsch the exact line of its telling, Ellicott the quiet weight it added to Esther's standing. And beneath their agreement lies the point the chapter has been building toward: that the same channel opened by a guardian's daily walk now carries a king's life in its keeping, and lays up, in the royal records, a debt to Mordecai that will be called in at the very hour the Jews stand in most need.
23:
The chapter ends on justice done and a record made, and the witnesses read in that record the seed of all that will follow. The reformed John Gill notes that when inquisition was made the matter was found out: full proof was given that the two men had indeed conspired against the king's life, and on that proof, the two being convicted, they suffered. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers on the manner of their death, taking the "hanging on a tree" to be impaling — a pointed stake set upright and the condemned drawn down upon it, a dreadful punishment under which the victim lived long in agony. Clarke also seizes the occasion to answer an old reproach against the book, that the name of God never once occurs in it: true, he grants, of the Hebrew and every version from it, yet the Septuagint supplies at v.20 the words that Mordecai had charged Esther "to fear God and keep his commandments," so that the divine name is not wholly absent, and its silence elsewhere was surely not for want of fair occasion.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same execution as crucifixion, a common Persian punishment for rebels, and recalls that Xerxes had the dead body of Leonidas crucified after Thermopylae. The "book of the chronicles," he adds, is that Persian record to which Herodotus so often refers — and it is precisely there, he hints, that a sleepless night of the king will one day, by seeming accident, light again upon Mordecai's forgotten service.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the proof and the sentence, Clarke the horror of the death and the vindication of the book's piety, Ellicott the mode of execution and the fateful register in which the deed was written down. And all of them feel the weight the closing clause is meant to carry: that Mordecai's name was set in the king's own chronicle, unrewarded for the present, but recorded — a debt entered in a book that will be opened again at the exact moment it can save a people. The chapter that opened with a banquet and a search for a queen closes with a stake and a written line; and the witnesses leave the reader knowing that the quiet entry in the annals, more than the crown or the feast, is the hinge on which the deliverance still to come will turn.
